claim: Borophagine canids have long been hypothesized to be North American ecological 'avatars' of living hyenas in Africa and Asia.
source: Borophagine canids have long been hypothesized to be North American ecological 'avatars' of living hyenas in Africa and Asia, but direct fossil evidence of hyena-like bone consumption is hitherto unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about existing hypotheses in the scientific literature regarding the ecological role of borophagine canids.

claim: Direct fossil evidence of hyena-like bone consumption in borophagine canids was previously unknown.
source: Borophagine canids have long been hypothesized to be North American ecological 'avatars' of living hyenas in Africa and Asia, but direct fossil evidence of hyena-like bone consumption is hitherto unknown.
evidence: This statement describes the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Rare coprolites of Borophagus parvus were found in the late Miocene of California.
source: We report rare coprolites (fossilized feces) of Borophagus parvus from the late Miocene of California and, for the first time, describe unambiguous evidence that these predatory canids ingested large amounts of bone.
evidence: This is a direct report of the discovery of fossil specimens from a specific location and time period.

claim: The coprolites provide the first unambiguous evidence that Borophagus parvus ingested large amounts of bone.
source: We report rare coprolites (fossilized feces) of Borophagus parvus from the late Miocene of California and, for the first time, describe unambiguous evidence that these predatory canids ingested large amounts of bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of coprolite contents presented in the manuscript.

claim: The coprolites show droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans.
source: Surface morphology, micro-CT analyses, and contextual information reveal (1) droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans
evidence: This is based on the spatial distribution of coprolites at the locality and comparison to modern carnivoran behavior.

claim: Borophagus parvus routinely consumed skeletons.
source: Surface morphology, micro-CT analyses, and contextual information reveal (1) droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans; (2) routine consumption of skeletons
evidence: This is inferred from the abundance of bone fragments found within the coprolites.

claim: Undissolved bones inside coprolites indicate gastrointestinal similarity to modern striped and brown hyenas.
source: Surface morphology, micro-CT analyses, and contextual information reveal (1) droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans; (2) routine consumption of skeletons; (3) undissolved bones inside coprolites indicating gastrointestinal similarity to modern striped and brown hyenas
evidence: This is based on comparison of bone fragment preservation in the coprolites to known digestive patterns in modern hyenas.

claim: Borophagus parvus had a body weight of approximately 24 kg.
source: Surface morphology, micro-CT analyses, and contextual information reveal (1) droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans; (2) routine consumption of skeletons; (3) undissolved bones inside coprolites indicating gastrointestinal similarity to modern striped and brown hyenas; (4) B. parvus body weight of ~24 kg, reaching sizes of obligatory large-prey hunters
evidence: This is calculated from measurements of skeletal elements using regression equations.

claim: Borophagus parvus reached sizes of obligatory large-prey hunters.
source: Surface morphology, micro-CT analyses, and contextual information reveal (1) droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans; (2) routine consumption of skeletons; (3) undissolved bones inside coprolites indicating gastrointestinal similarity to modern striped and brown hyenas; (4) B. parvus body weight of ~24 kg, reaching sizes of obligatory large-prey hunters
evidence: This is inferred from body mass estimates and comparison to modern carnivoran ecology.

claim: Prey size of Borophagus parvus ranged approximately 35–100 kg.
source: Surface morphology, micro-CT analyses, and contextual information reveal (1) droppings in concentrations signifying scent-marking behavior, similar to latrines used by living social carnivorans; (2) routine consumption of skeletons; (3) undissolved bones inside coprolites indicating gastrointestinal similarity to modern striped and brown hyenas; (4) B. parvus body weight of ~24 kg, reaching sizes of obligatory large-prey hunters; and (5) prey size ranging ~35–100 kg.
evidence: This is estimated from measurements of bone fragments in coprolites compared to modern ungulate skeletons.

claim: Bone-crushing Borophagus potentially hunted in collaborative social groups.
source: This combination of traits suggests that bone-crushing Borophagus potentially hunted in collaborative social groups and occupied a niche no longer present in North American ecosystems.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including latrine behavior, body size, and prey size.

claim: Borophagus occupied a niche no longer present in North American ecosystems.
source: This combination of traits suggests that bone-crushing Borophagus potentially hunted in collaborative social groups and occupied a niche no longer present in North American ecosystems.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of Borophagus morphology and behavior to modern North American carnivorans.

claim: Several lineages of dogs and hyenas have independently evolved bone-crushing adaptations.
source: Several lineages of dogs (family Canidae) and hyenas (family Hyaenidae) have independently evolved striking bone-crushing adaptations, such as highly robust skulls, jaws, teeth, and large attachment areas for powerful masticatory muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about convergent evolution in carnivorans.

claim: Bone-crushing morphologies are likely associated with social hunting.
source: These highly specialized bone-cracking morphologies are likely associated with social hunting (Van Valkenburgh and Koepfli, 1993; Van Valkenburgh et al., 2003), as best exemplified by the living spotted hyena (Kruuk, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on carnivoran ecology.

claim: Spotted hyenas hunt and feed in groups.
source: Spotted hyenas hunt and feed in groups, have a gastrointestinal system that is able to break down large quantities of bone consumed, and discharge feces with high-carbonate content (Macdonald, 1978; Estes, 1991; Hulsman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spotted hyena behavior supported by citations.

claim: Spotted hyenas have a gastrointestinal system that is able to break down large quantities of bone.
source: Spotted hyenas hunt and feed in groups, have a gastrointestinal system that is able to break down large quantities of bone consumed, and discharge feces with high-carbonate content (Macdonald, 1978; Estes, 1991; Hulsman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spotted hyena physiology supported by citations.

claim: Spotted hyenas discharge feces with high-carbonate content.
source: Spotted hyenas hunt and feed in groups, have a gastrointestinal system that is able to break down large quantities of bone consumed, and discharge feces with high-carbonate content (Macdonald, 1978; Estes, 1991; Hulsman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about spotted hyena feces supported by citations.

claim: Borophagines are a group of carnivorans with highly specialized craniodental morphological traits indicative of bone-cracking adaptation.
source: Borophagines are a group of carnivorans with highly specialized craniodental morphological traits indicative of bone-cracking adaptation, and have long been recognized to be a terminal member of the subfamily Borophaginae that went extinct just before the beginning of the Ice Ages in North America (Wang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about borophagine morphology supported by citation.

claim: Borophagines went extinct just before the beginning of the Ice Ages in North America.
source: Borophagines are a group of carnivorans with highly specialized craniodental morphological traits indicative of bone-cracking adaptation, and have long been recognized to be a terminal member of the subfamily Borophaginae that went extinct just before the beginning of the Ice Ages in North America (Wang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about borophagine extinction timing supported by citation.

claim: The coprolites were discovered from the Mehrten Formation (latest Miocene, 5.3–6.4 Ma) in Stanislaus County, California.
source: We analyzed a new sample of coprolites recently discovered from the Mehrten Formation (latest Miocene, 5.3–6.4 Ma) in Stanislaus County, California.
evidence: This is a direct report of the geological context of the specimens.

claim: Numerous bone fragments on the external surface and inside the coprolites strongly suggest that they were produced by Borophagus.
source: Numerous bone fragments on the external surface and inside the coprolites strongly suggest that they were produced by Borophagus, which is amply represented by body fossils at the same fossil-producing area, thereby affording a rare opportunity to directly examine the diet of an extinct bone-crushing top predator.
evidence: This is based on the presence of bone fragments in coprolites and the abundance of Borophagus fossils at the locality.

claim: Borophagus is amply represented by body fossils at the same fossil-producing area as the coprolites.
source: Numerous bone fragments on the external surface and inside the coprolites strongly suggest that they were produced by Borophagus, which is amply represented by body fossils at the same fossil-producing area, thereby affording a rare opportunity to directly examine the diet of an extinct bone-crushing top predator.
evidence: This is a statement about the fossil record at the locality.

claim: Dietary inferences for borophagines were previously made only from the fossilized bones of these predators.
source: Despite improvements in our understanding of the biomechanics of the functional convergence of craniodental adaptations between Eurasian-African hyaenids and North American borophagine canids (Werdelin, 1989; Tseng and Wang, 2010; Tseng and Wang, 2011), dietary inferences were previously made only from the fossilized bones of these predators.
evidence: This describes the state of knowledge prior to the discovery of coprolites.

claim: The study examines 14 coprolites recovered from two localities in the Turlock Lake area.
source: This study examines 14 coprolites recovered from two localities in the Turlock Lake area, as well as their presumed producer, Borophagus parvus.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and provenance.

claim: The large number of bones inside most Mehrten coprolites rules out herbivores as their producers.
source: The large number of bones inside most Mehrten coprolites rules out herbivores as their producers.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the contents of the coprolites.

claim: The size of the coprolites indicates large carnivorans as their original makers.
source: The size of the coprolites further indicates large carnivorans as their original makers.
evidence: This is inferred from measurements of coprolite dimensions.

claim: Wagner (1976, 1981) listed a bone-crushing dog Borophagus secundus (=Osteoborus cyonoides), a small coyote-sized Eucyon davisi, an ancestral badger Pliotaxidea garberi, an early wolverine Plesiogulo marshalli, and an ancestral cat Pseudaelurus near P. hibbardi as medium to large carnivorans from the Mehrten Formation.
source: For medium to large carnivorans from the Mehrten Formation, Wagner (1976, 1981) listed a bone-crushing dog Borophagus secundus (=Osteoborus cyonoides), a small coyote-sized Eucyon davisi, an ancestral badger Pliotaxidea garberi, an early wolverine Plesiogulo marshalli, and an ancestral cat Pseudaelurus near P. hibbardi.
evidence: This is a citation of previous work on the Mehrten fauna.

claim: Balisi et al. (2018) added a fox, Vulpes stenognathus, to the list of Mehrten carnivorans.
source: Most recently, Balisi et al. (2018) added a fox, Vulpes stenognathus, to the list.
evidence: This is a citation of recent work on the Mehrten fauna.

claim: Vulpes, Eucyon, Pliotaxidea, and Plesiogulo can be ruled out as being too small to produce scats of the size of the Mehrten coprolites.
source: Of the above, Vulpes, Eucyon, Pliotaxidea, and Plesiogulo can be ruled out as being too small to produce scats of the size of the Mehrten coprolites, whereas the true nature of Mehrten felids is poorly known.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of coprolite size to known body sizes of these taxa.

claim: Balisi et al. (2018) recognized two bone-crushing canids, B. secundus and B. parvus, which are the only wolf-sized taxa large enough to be the producers of the Mehrten coprolites.
source: Of the large Mehrten canids, Balisi et al. (2018) recognized two bone-crushing canids, B. secundus and B. parvus, which are the only wolf-sized taxa large enough to be the producers of the Mehrten coprolites.
evidence: This is based on citation of recent taxonomic work and size comparison.

claim: B. secundus is rare in the Mehrten Formation, represented by two fragmentary jaws and teeth plus 1–2 questionably referred teeth.
source: Of these two species, B. secundus is rare, represented by two fragmentary jaws and teeth plus 1–2 questionably referred teeth, whereas B. parvus is far better represented by 27 specimens.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative abundance of fossils in the collection.

claim: B. parvus is far better represented in the Mehrten Formation by 27 specimens.
source: Of these two species, B. secundus is rare, represented by two fragmentary jaws and teeth plus 1–2 questionably referred teeth, whereas B. parvus is far better represented by 27 specimens.
evidence: This is a statement about the relative abundance of fossils in the collection.

claim: The Mehrten coprolites are comparable in size to scats from extant wolves.
source: The Mehrten coprolites are comparable in size (Table 1) to scats from extant wolves and are generally larger than those from living coyotes, despite significant overlap between scat diameters of the wolves (average 27 mm, range 13–47 mm) and the coyotes (average 21 mm, range 7–34 mm) (Weaver and Fritts, 1979; Reid, 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of measurements in Table 1 to published data on modern carnivoran scats.

claim: Mehrten coprolites are generally larger than scats from living coyotes.
source: The Mehrten coprolites are comparable in size (Table 1) to scats from extant wolves and are generally larger than those from living coyotes, despite significant overlap between scat diameters of the wolves (average 27 mm, range 13–47 mm) and the coyotes (average 21 mm, range 7–34 mm) (Weaver and Fritts, 1979; Reid, 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of measurements in Table 1 to published data on modern carnivoran scats.

claim: Harrison (2011) documented scat diameters of 20–35 mm from African hunting dogs, Lycaon pictus, and striped hyena, Hyaena hyaena.
source: In extant African carnivores, Harrison (2011) documented scat diameters of 20–35 mm from African hunting dogs, Lycaon pictus, and striped hyena, Hyaena hyaena.
evidence: This is a citation of published data on modern carnivoran scat dimensions.

claim: With a maximum diameter of 31.2 mm, the Mehrten coprolites are more likely produced by a wolf-sized Borophagus than a coyote- to fox-sized Eucyon.
source: Therefore, with a maximum diameter of 31.2 mm, the Mehrten coprolites are more likely produced by a wolf-sized Borophagus than a coyote- to fox-sized Eucyon.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of coprolite size to modern carnivoran scat sizes.

claim: B. parvus was the more likely producer of Mehrten coprolites based on their body size and far better representation of body fossils.
source: Of the two species of Mehrten Borophagus, B. parvus was the more likely producers of Mehrten coprolites based on their body size and far better representation of body fossils, although the possibility of B. secundus cannot be excluded.
evidence: This is inferred from fossil abundance and size comparisons.

claim: Mehrten coprolites appear to share substantial similarities to those of living hyenas.
source: Although scat morphology of extant wolves and hyenas may be somewhat different—depending on length of retention in digestive tract, fiber and water content of feces, and hardness of ground on which scats were dropped—our Mehrten coprolites (Figures 2 and 3) appear to share substantial similarities to those of living hyenas (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on visual comparison of coprolite morphology to modern hyena scats shown in figures.

claim: Five of the 14 individually catalogued coprolites probably are a first dropping due to their bluntly constricted terminal on at least one of their ends and their relatively greater diameter.
source: Of the 14 individually catalogued coprolites, five probably are a first dropping due to their bluntly constricted terminal on at least one of their ends and their relatively greater diameter (LACM 158707, 158708, 158709, 158711, and 158712).
evidence: This is inferred from morphological characteristics of the coprolites.

claim: Only LACM 158709 has the typical shape of a conical pellet.
source: However, only one, LACM 158709, has the typical shape of a conical pellet (Figure 1A), although LACM 158707 represents a variation of the conical-disk pellet combination that failed to separate after dropping.
evidence: This is based on morphological description of individual specimens.

claim: The Mehrten coprolite sample probably consists of individual pellets from multiple dropping events possibly by multiple individuals.
source: If the above assessment is correct, the Mehrten coprolite sample probably consists of individual pellets from multiple dropping events possibly by multiple individuals.
evidence: This is inferred from variation in coprolite morphology and preservation.

claim: Different degrees of desiccation among different coprolite pellets suggest they were not defecated at the same time.
source: This is also suggested by different degrees of desiccation among different coprolite pellets (Figure 5E), that is, they were not defecated at the same time.
evidence: This is inferred from observed variation in surface cracking shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The LACM 3937 locality may have been an ancient 'latrine' ground for social defecating and scent-marking for territorial boundaries.
source: If this is the case, and assuming that the coprolites have not been transported (there is no sign for transportation), the LACM 3937 locality may have been an ancient 'latrine' ground for social defecating and scent-marking for territorial boundaries.
evidence: This is inferred from the concentration of coprolites at the locality and comparison to modern carnivoran behavior.

claim: Latrine locations have been well documented in extant spotted hyenas (Kruuk, 1972), coyotes (Gese and Ruff, 1997), and wolves (Asa et al., 1985; Harrington and Asa, 2003).
source: Such locations have been well documented in extant spotted hyenas (Kruuk, 1972), coyotes (Gese and Ruff, 1997), and wolves (Asa et al., 1985; Harrington and Asa, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about modern carnivoran behavior supported by citations.

claim: Latrine behavior has not been documented in extinct carnivorans prior to this study.
source: While such behavior is common among social carnivorans, it has not been documented in extinct carnivorans.
evidence: This describes the novelty of the finding in the context of paleontology.

claim: Mehrten coprolites maintain nearly perfectly rounded cross sections, showing no sign of post-defecation settling or flattening.
source: Mehrten coprolites maintain nearly perfectly rounded cross sections, showing no sign of post-defecation settling or flattening, nor is there any sign of deformation during the initial impact of dropping.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of the specimens.

claim: The original feces were able to maintain their integrity either because of a relatively hard, moisture-free matrix, and/or because the bones inside plus the high-calcareous contents of the matrix resulted in relatively rigid feces at defecation.
source: This suggests that the original feces were able to maintain their integrity either because of a relatively hard, moisture-free matrix, and/or because the bones inside plus the high-calcareous contents of the matrix resulted in relatively rigid feces at defecation.
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation state of the coprolites.

claim: The coprolites show no major signs of post-defecation alteration, suggesting fast burial after dropping.
source: Nor do the coprolites show major signs of post-defecation alteration, suggesting fast burial after dropping.
evidence: This is inferred from the preservation state of the coprolites.

claim: Bones are abundant in all coprolites, consisting of 5% of total volume of all coprolites (range 2–25%).
source: Bones are abundant in all coprolites, consisting of 5% of total volume of all coprolites (range 2–25%; see Table 1 for individual volume estimates).
evidence: This is calculated from micro-CT analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: LACM 158707 is a nearly perfectly preserved coprolite and also one of the largest, measuring 31.2 mm in maximum diameter.
source: This is a nearly perfectly preserved coprolite and also one of the largest, measuring 31.2 mm in maximum diameter.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of a specimen.

claim: LACM 158707 is composed of two unseparated pellets, as delineated by a visible groove.
source: This coprolite is composed of two unseparated pellets, as delineated by a visible groove.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation of the specimen.

claim: At least 14 bone fragments are recognizable in CT image of LACM 158707, although all are unidentifiable small pieces.
source: A single bone is visible on the external surface, with at least 14 bone fragments recognizable in CT image (Figure 2D), although all are unidentifiable small pieces.
evidence: This is based on micro-CT analysis of the specimen shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LACM 158708 contains the largest piece of bone, a fragment of a rib shaft measuring 29 mm long × 9.2 mm wide × 5.1 mm thick.
source: This coprolite also contains the largest piece of bone, a fragment of a rib shaft measuring 29 mm long × 9.2 mm wide × 5.1 mm thick, that nearly spans the length of the pellet (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is based on micro-CT analysis and measurements of the specimen.

claim: The terminal end of the rib in LACM 158708 protrudes outside the coprolite on the tapered end, leaving a sharp tip, 3 mm long, projecting at an angle into the lateral wall of the intestine and showing modest polishing on its surface.
source: The terminal end of this rib also protrudes outside the coprolite on the tapered end, leaving a sharp tip, 3 mm long, projecting at an angle into the lateral wall of the intestine and showing modest polishing on its surface (red arrows in Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on observation of the specimen shown in Figure 3.

claim: Total bone volume is 13% of coprolite matrix for LACM 158708, among the highest of all coprolites.
source: Total bone volume is 13% of coprolite matrix for LACM 158708, among the highest of all coprolites (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from micro-CT analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: The majority of bones inside the coprolites are too small and too fragmentary to be identified to a particular element or to a particular taxon beyond mammals or even vertebrates.
source: The majority of bones inside the coprolites, even when fully exposed, are too small and too fragmentary to be identified to a particular element or to a particular taxon beyond mammals or even vertebrates.
evidence: This is based on examination of bone fragments in the coprolites.

claim: With the exception of a single rib fragment in LACM 158708, all other virtually segmented bones lack sufficient morphological detail to be unambiguously identified.
source: With the exception of a single rib fragment in LACM 158708, all other virtually segmented bones lack sufficient morphological detail to be unambiguously identified.
evidence: This is based on micro-CT analysis of the specimens.

claim: There is a lack of clear orientation of bones relative to the long axis of each coprolite.
source: Generally, there is a lack of clear orientation relative to the long axis of each coprolite (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of bone orientations shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lack of a longitudinal orientation may be due to a relatively viscous (low water content) matrix and compaction during the last (dehydration) journey of feces through the large intestine.
source: Lack of a longitudinal orientation may also be due to a relatively viscous (low water content) matrix and compaction during the last (dehydration) journey of feces through the large intestine.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed random orientation of bones.

claim: Surface modifications on bones include rounding of corners, polishing of surface, and acid etching.
source: Surface modifications on bones include rounding of corners, polishing of surface, and acid etching.
evidence: This is based on observation of bone surfaces in the coprolites.

claim: About 5% of bones recovered from living wolf scat can be identified to their prey species (Fosse et al., 2012).
source: About 5% of bones recovered from living wolf scat can be identified to their prey species (Fosse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a citation of published data on modern wolf scats.

claim: Four bone fragments from Mehrten coprolites, consisting of 8% of the total number of bone fragments, preserve enough original morphology to be narrowed to more specific taxa or anatomic structure.
source: Four bone fragments from Mehrten coprolites, consisting of 8% of the total number of bone fragments (Table 1), preserve enough original morphology to be narrowed to more specific taxa or anatomic structure.
evidence: This is based on examination of bone fragments and data in Table 1.

claim: A large piece of bone in LACM 158711 has thin walls and hollow internal structure likely belonging to a bird limb bone.
source: A large piece of bone, measuring at least 6.0 × 3.6 mm in cross-sectional area, has thin walls and hollow internal structure likely belonging to a bird limb bone.
evidence: This is inferred from morphological characteristics of the bone fragment.

claim: The only fossil bird so far reported from the Modesto Reservoir Member is a goose, Branta (Wagner, 1981).
source: The only fossil bird so far reported from the Modesto Reservoir Member is a goose, Branta (Wagner, 1981).
evidence: This is a citation of previous work on the Mehrten fauna.

claim: A very large flat bone in LACM 158712 resembles the ascending ramus of a beaver.
source: A very large flat bone, resembling the ascending ramus of a beaver, spans the width of the coprolite.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison of the bone fragment.

claim: Two beavers, Castor californicus and Dipoides vallicula, are both known in the Mehrten Formation (Wagner, 1981).
source: Two beavers, Castor californicus and Dipoides vallicula, are both known in the Mehrten Formation (Wagner, 1981) and belong to the semiaquatic beaver clade (Rybczynski, 2007).
evidence: This is a citation of previous work on the Mehrten fauna.

claim: Semiaquatic beavers possess a highly diagnostic backwardly hooked ascending ramus (coronoid process) that is possibly related to woodcutting behavior.
source: All of them possess a highly diagnostic backwardly hooked ascending ramus (coronoid process; see comparison with that of Eucastor tortus in Figure 5G, an extant species adjacent to Dipoides in the beaver phylogeny) that is possibly related to woodcutting behavior.
evidence: This is based on morphological observation and comparison shown in Figure 5G, with speculation about functional significance.

claim: Modern wolves typically feed on the internal organs first—such as the heart, lungs, and liver (Stahler et al., 2006).
source: Modern wolves typically feed on the internal organs first—such as the heart, lungs, and liver (Stahler et al., 2006)—and the ribcage is the main obstacle to reaching the organs.
evidence: This is a citation of published data on modern wolf feeding behavior.

claim: Experimental data on modern gray wolf diet and their scat permit a certain measure of quantifying scat contents and identifying prey items.
source: Experimental data on modern gray wolf diet and their scat permit a certain measure of quantifying scat contents and identifying prey items.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of modern analogs for interpreting fossil evidence.

claim: A study on bone fragments preserved in extant Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus) scat provides a valuable basis for comparison (Esteban-Nadal et al., 2010).
source: A study on bone fragments preserved in extant Iberian wolf (Canis lupus signatus) scat provides a valuable basis for comparison (Esteban-Nadal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a citation of a study used for comparative analysis.

claim: More than 80% of bone fragments in Iberian wolf scat are not identifiable to a particular bone or taxon.
source: More than 80% of bone fragments in Iberian wolf scat are not identifiable to a particular bone or taxon.
evidence: This is a statement about published data on modern wolf scats.

claim: A study of Polish wolves had a 95% rate of unidentified bones (Fosse et al., 2012).
source: A study of Polish wolves had a 95% rate of unidentified bones (Fosse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a citation of published data on modern wolf scats.

claim: 92% of bones in Mehrten canid coprolites are unidentified.
source: The same is true for Mehrten canid coprolites: four relatively large bones are identified among 48 in total (i.e. 92% unidentified bones).
evidence: This is calculated from the data on bone identification in the coprolites.

claim: Sizes of individual bone fragments in scat of extant wolves are roughly comparable to those in the Mehrten coprolites.
source: Finally, sizes of individual bone fragments in scat of extant wolves are also roughly comparable to those in our fossils.
evidence: This is based on comparison of bone fragment sizes.

claim: Borophagus and bone-cracking hyaenids such as Crocuta share several craniodental features that have been interpreted as adaptations for a durophagous diet.
source: Borophagus and bone-cracking hyaenids such as Crocuta share several craniodental features that have been interpreted as adaptations for a durophagous diet.
evidence: This is established knowledge about convergent evolution in these taxa.

claim: Upper and lower dentitions of both Borophagus and Crocuta exhibit specialized enamel microstructure (Hunter-Schreger Bands) of the cheek teeth interpreted to represent evolutionary responses to resisting increasingly hard and abrasive foods (Rensberger and Wang, 2005; Tseng, 2011).
source: Upper and lower dentitions of both taxa also exhibit specialized enamel microstructure (Hunter-Schreger Bands) of the cheek teeth interpreted to represent evolutionary responses to resisting increasingly hard and abrasive foods (Rensberger and Wang, 2005; Tseng, 2011).
evidence: This is based on cited studies of enamel microstructure.

claim: In both dental morphology and enamel microstructure, Borophagus and Crocuta share more similarities to each other than to Canis.
source: In both dental morphology and enamel microstructure, Borophagus and Crocuta share more similarities to each other than to Canis (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is based on comparative morphological analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Macrowear analyses demonstrate that the extant bone-cracking Crocuta exhibits much more extreme cusp wear on average than either Canis or Borophagus (DeSantis et al., 2017).
source: However, macrowear analyses of the lower carnassial tooth (m1) in population samples of the three carnivorans demonstrate that the extant bone-cracking Crocuta exhibits much more extreme cusp wear on average than either Canis or Borophagus (DeSantis et al., 2017) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on cited macrowear analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Comparisons of overall stress distributions during unilateral carnassial (P4) bite simulations using finite element analysis indicate that the crania of Crocuta and Borophagus are more similar to each other in exhibiting lower and more dissipated stress patterns than Canis (Tseng, 2011).
source: Lastly, comparisons of overall stress distributions during unilateral carnassial (P4) bite simulations using finite element analysis indicate that the crania of Crocuta and Borophagus are more similar to each other in exhibiting lower and more dissipated stress patterns than Canis (Tseng, 2011) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on cited finite element analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Bones as a supplementary food source must be a net gain if the cost of processing bones (both ingestion and digestion) can be managed.
source: Bones as a supplementary food source must be a net gain if the cost of processing bones (both ingestion and digestion) can be managed.
evidence: This is a logical statement about energetics of bone consumption.

claim: The average compact bone consists of about 30% organic matrix (Eastoe and Eastoe, 1954; Guyton and Hall, 2006), mostly collagen fibers.
source: The average compact bone consists of about 30% organic matrix (Eastoe and Eastoe, 1954; Guyton and Hall, 2006), mostly collagen fibers.
